newsitem.title: USA: Irish punt/Ffranc divergence raises new ERM worry.
newsitem.headline: Irish punt/Ffranc divergence raises new ERM worry.

text.p: The divergence between the Irish punt and the French franc, which is nearing the 15-percent limit allowed by Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM), may unleash foreign exchange fireworks after France's Bastille Day, traders and analysts said on Monday.

"Something is going to have to give here," said J.P. Morgan global currency strategist Ron Leven, commenting on the 12.90-percent divergence between the strongest and weakest ERM currencies. Trading in the French franc was thin with French banks closed on Monday for the national holiday.

The European Union widened the ERM fluctuation bands during a European monetary crisis in 1993 from 2.25 percent to 15 percent. Since then, fluctuations have never reached the 15-percent limit that would trigger mandatory European central banks' intervention.

"The Bank of France and the central bank of Ireland would have to intervene if we go to the 15-percent limit on the ERM band. They don't have a choice, it's mandatory intervention," a foreign exchange trader at a French bank said.
The Irish and French currencies are also violating another measure of currency stability -- the ERM divergence indicator.
On Monday, the punt stood at a reading of plus 63 and the franc at minus 21, beyond the maximum 75-point divergence allowed between two ERM currencies.
The trader said this raised the odds for French and Irish intervention when trading resumes in Paris on Tuesday.
But J.P. Morgan's Leven stressed central bank intervention woould not solve the fundamental issues tied to the strong punt.
"The Irish punt is pulled between its two links, pulled between its intention to be part of the euro and its historical ties with the United Kingdom," Leven said.

The Irish punt is lifted by the strength in sterling which rose on Monday to its highest level versus the mark since October 1990. Britain is Ireland's largest trading partner and left the ERM in September 1992.
Also, the booming Irish economy is raising concern about inflation pressures and talk of higher interest rates.
"Ireland will have to do something to get the punt back toward its ERM level, like devalue it, or they will have to give up being part of the euro," Leven also said.
Ireland is one of the few European countries that meets the Maastricht criteria to qualify for the euro. However, the punt must remain within the ERM parameters until the euro launch.
Andrew Hodge, vice president at Bank Brussels Lambert, agreed the punt's strength highlighted fundamental issues tied to Ireland's ties with Britain and continental Europe.
"The Irish better figure out now how to deal with these problems now because the problems won't go away if they join the euro and the UK does not," Hodge said.
One way for Ireland to solve the 15-percent rule problem would be to raise its parity within the ERM -- a revaluation that would hurt its foreign trade.

"You can't rule that out but I see the odds of a punt revaluation at less than 10 percent," Hodge said. "They could also request a temporary dispensation from the 15-percent rule and wait for sterling to return to lower levels which would take the punt lower as well."
The mark is another currency in danger of reaching its ERM limits versus the punt, with a divergence indicator beyond the 75-point rule.
"The 15-percent rule was created for a band so wide nobody would ever think we would get there. But here we are," Hodge noted.
